vulns.description: ## Summary Bleach 6.3.0 exposes a documented email-linkification path through `bleach.linkify(..., parse_email=True)`. The implementation scans attacker-controlled text with `EMAIL_RE.finditer()` over the full character token and has no length, timeout, or linear prefilter before applying the dot-atom email regex. A non-email payload around 30 KB causes multi-second CPU consumption per request/call, creating a direct availability risk for applications that enable email linkification on user-submitted text.  ## Affected Product - Package: `bleach` - Ecosystem: pip - Affected versions: verified in `6.3.0`; exact first affected version not established - Patched versions: none known at finalization time - Tested version: `6.3.0` - Audit commit/tag: `v6.3.0` / `5546d5dbce60d08ccb99d981778d74044d646d4e` - PyPI sdist SHA256: `6f3b91b1c0a02bb9a78b5a454c92506aa0fdf197e1d5e114d2e00c6f64306d22`  ## Vulnerability Details - CWE: CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity; related availability impact maps to CWE-400 - Component: `bleach/linkifier.py`, `build_email_re()`, `LinkifyFilter.handle_email_addresses()` - Root cause: `handle_email_addresses()` calls `self.email_re.finditer(text)` on attacker-controlled text. `EMAIL_RE` includes a repeated dot-atom local-part pattern, so non-email strings such as repeated `a.` segments with no `@` force repeated long failing scans. - Security boundary violated: user-submitted text processed by a documented safe linkification helper should not allow an attacker to impose superlinear CPU cost through non-email text. - Direct impact: per-request CPU exhaustion / denial-of-service risk in applications that enable `parse_email=True` on attacker-controlled text. - Chain impact, if any: one proof run observed an unrelated `/health` request delayed during a concurrent attack request, but this was not reliable across reviewer retests. Treat cross-request service degradation as environment-dependent supporting evidence, not the primary impact. - Severity estimate: Medium / availability-only. The feature is opt-in and deployment body limits/timeouts affect practical severity.  Relevant code path: - `bleach/__init__.py:85-125`: public `linkify(text, ..., parse_email=False)` constructs `Linker(..., parse_email=parse_email)` and calls `linker.linkify(text)`. - `bleach/linkifier.py:77-88`: `EMAIL_RE` is compiled from the dot-atom email pattern. - `bleach/linkifier.py:292-301`: `handle_email_addresses()` applies `self.email_re.finditer(text)` to each character token. - `bleach/linkifier.py:620-623`: character tokens are routed into email handling only when `parse_email` is true. - `docs/goals.rst:30-40`: Bleach documents user comments, profile bios, and descriptions as target untrusted text use cases. - `docs/linkify.rst:300-305`: `parse_email=True` is the documented option for creating `mailto:` links.  ## Attack Preconditions - The consuming application enables the documented `parse_email=True` option, for example `bleach.linkify(user_text, parse_email=True)` or `Linker(parse_email=True).linkify(user_text)`. - The attacker can submit text that reaches that linkification path. Authentication depends on the host application; a public comment form would make this unauthenticated, while account-only text fields require user privileges. - The application allows roughly 20-30 KB of text to reach Bleach and lacks a strict timeout or input cap before linkification. - No custom bounded `email_re` is supplied.  ## Reproduction Minimal API trigger:  ```python import bleach payload = ("a." * 15000) + "a" bleach.linkify(payload, parse_email=True) ```  The saved HTTP proof uses a local harness with `POST /preview` calling `bleach.linkify(request_body, parse_email=True)` and a control endpoint using `parse_email=False` on the same payload. The exploit sends baseline/control/attack requests over HTTP to `127.0.0.1`.  ## Proof Evidence The proof ran against Bleach `6.3.0` installed from the audited local checkout in an isolated temporary venv. It used Python `3.12.3` on Linux.  Measured HTTP proof results: - Payload: `("a." * 15000) + "a"` (`30001` bytes) - Normal baseline `/preview` mean: `0.001425` seconds - Same 30 KB payload with `parse_email=False`: `0.048349` seconds - Attack payload with `parse_email=True`: `8.719818` seconds - Slowdown versus the larger baseline/control mean: `180.35x` - Requests sent by proof: `20`  Evidence files: [poc.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27129729/poc.py) [poc_results.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27129737/poc_results.json) [exploit_proof.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27129751/exploit_proof.py) [exploit_results.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27129752/exploit_results.json)  ## Scope and Limitations - This report does not claim XSS, authentication bypass, data disclosure, remote code execution, persistent crash, or persistent service outage. - `parse_email=True` is not the default. The affected path is a documented opt-in feature. - The exact first affected version is not established. - Practical impact depends on host application input limits, worker model, request timeout policy, and whether untrusted users can submit text to an email-linkification path. - A reviewer reproduced the direct CPU cost but did not reproduce the proof harness’s `/health` delay. The direct impact claim is therefore limited to per-request CPU exhaustion. - Bleach is marked deprecated in `README.rst`, and `SECURITY.md` has stale supported-version text, but the package still has a 2025 PyPI release and published Mozilla security reporting routes.

### Summary  Bleach `clean()` / `Cleaner()` fails to sanitize dangerous URI schemes in allowed `formaction` attributes.  Bleach applies URI protocol sanitization only to attributes listed in `attr_val_is_uri`. While URI-bearing attributes such as `action`, `href`, `src`, and `poster` are included in that set, `formaction` is not. As a result, if a downstream application explicitly allows `formaction` on submit-capable controls in untrusted HTML, Bleach preserves dangerous values such as `javascript:alert(1)` instead of stripping them.  This can lead to **submit-triggered JavaScript execution** in applications that rely on Bleach to sanitize untrusted HTML and allow the relevant tag/attribute combination.  ---  ### Details  The issue appears to be a URI-sanitization coverage gap in Bleach’s sanitizer logic.  Relevant code paths:  * `bleach/sanitizer.py` — `BleachSanitizerFilter.allow_token` (around line 553) * `bleach/_vendor/html5lib/filters/sanitizer.py` — `attr_val_is_uri` (around line 525)  In `BleachSanitizerFilter.allow_token`, URI protocol sanitization is only applied when:  ```python id="pft79m" if namespaced_name in self.attr_val_is_uri: ```  However, `(None, 'formaction')` is currently missing from `attr_val_is_uri`.  This creates an inconsistency where `action` is protocol-sanitized, but `formaction` is not.  As a result, if a downstream application allows:  * tags such as `<button>` or `<input>` * the `formaction` attribute  then Bleach preserves dangerous URI schemes such as `javascript:` in `formaction`.  Examples of affected submit-capable controls include:  * `<button>` (default submit behavior unless `type="button"` is set) * `<input type="submit">` * `<input type="image">`  This appears to be a real library-side sanitizer gap rather than only an application misuse issue, because Bleach already treats similar URI-bearing attributes (such as `action`) as protocol-sensitive and sanitizes them.  Suggested minimal fix:  Add:  ```python id="4v4fkn" (None, 'formaction') ```  to `attr_val_is_uri` in:  * `bleach/_vendor/html5lib/filters/sanitizer.py`  I also prepared a minimal patch and focused regression tests if helpful.  ---  ### PoC  Below are minimal reproductions using `bleach.clean()`.  #### 1) `<button>`  ```python id="d3g0v7" from bleach import clean  print(clean(     '<form><button formaction="javascript:alert(1)">go</button></form>',     tags={'form', 'button'},     attributes={'button': ['formaction']}, )) ```  **Actual output:**  ```html id="i4nd7s" <form><button formaction="javascript:alert(1)">go</button></form> ```  **Expected output:**  ```html id="g4d2r1" <form><button>go</button></form> ```  ---  #### 2) `<input type="submit">`  ```python id="l4dy0j" print(clean(     '<form><input type="submit" formaction="javascript:alert(1)" value="go"></form>',     tags={'form', 'input'},     attributes={'input': ['type', 'formaction', 'value']}, )) ```  **Actual output:**  ```html id="h8lgbt" <form><input type="submit" formaction="javascript:alert(1)" value="go"></form> ```  **Expected output:**  ```html id="6y8mws" <form><input type="submit" value="go"></form> ```  ---  #### 3) `<input type="image">`  ```python id="g8q0x8" print(clean(     '<form><input type="image" formaction="javascript:alert(1)" src="/foo.png"></form>',     tags={'form', 'input'},     attributes={'input': ['type', 'formaction', 'src']}, )) ```  **Actual output:**  ```html id="fd22kg" <form><input type="image" formaction="javascript:alert(1)" src="/foo.png"></form> ```  **Expected output:**  ```html id="z6t6je" <form><input type="image" src="/foo.png"></form> ```  ---  ### Impact  This is a **client-side HTML sanitization bypass / dangerous URI preservation issue**.  If an application relies on Bleach to sanitize untrusted HTML and explicitly allows:  * `formaction` * and submit-capable controls such as `<button>` or `<input>`  then Bleach can emit sanitized output that still contains a dangerous `javascript:` URI in `formaction`.  That can lead to **submit-triggered JavaScript execution** when the user activates the control.  Impact is limited to configurations that explicitly allow the relevant tag/attribute combination, but the issue is still security-relevant because:  * `formaction` is a real browser sink * Bleach already protocol-sanitizes similar URI-bearing attributes like `action` * the omission creates inconsistent sanitizer coverage for dangerous URI schemes  I would currently assess this as **Medium severity**.  If useful, I also have:  * a minimal patch * focused regression tests for:    * `<button formaction="javascript:...">`   * `<input type="submit" formaction="javascript:...">`   * `<input type="image" formaction="javascript:...">`   * a safe control case where `formaction="/submit"` is preserved

### Impact A possible XSS bypass affects users calling `bleach.clean` with all of: * `a` in the allowed tags * `href` in allowed attributes The `bleach.clean` sanitizer outputs URIs containing disallowed scheme patterns that it should be stripping. However, because the inserted Unicode characters make the scheme invalid per RFC 3986, modern browsers do not execute these as javascript: URIs. The practical security impact is limited to: - Bleach's output contains URI values that violate the caller's protocol allowlist, breaking the sanitizer's contract. - If a downstream system performs its own Unicode normalization on bleach's output (stripping invisible characters before rendering), the javascript: scheme could become valid. This is a non-standard processing chain but represents a theoretical secondary risk. This is not a direct XSS vulnerability. Python code example from reporter with Bleach v6.3.0 and Python 3.13: ``` import bleach payload1 = 'Click me' result1 = bleach.clean(payload1) print(f"(ZWSP): {repr(result1)}") ``` Output: ``` (ZWSP): 'Click me' ``` ### Patches Users should upgrade to Bleach 6.4.0. ### Workarounds Pre-process content removing non-ASCII characters from URI schemes before sanitizing with `bleach.clean`. A strong[ Content-Security-Policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CSP) without unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval[ script-srcs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/script-src) will also help mitigate the risk. ### References * https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2023812 * RFC 3986, Section 3.1 (URI Scheme syntax): scheme characters are restricted to ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." ) ### Reported by Reported by codeant from CodeAnt AI.

### Summary   `create_submodule(name, path, url)` clones a submodule into the repo's own `.git` directory before it rejects the path. A `path` of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory, and a file named `post-checkout` in the submodule becomes an executable `.git/hooks/post-checkout`. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise `ValueError`, but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.  ### Details   The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk. This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.  Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict check only reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:  git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add)   599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path)           # accepts ".git/hooks"   673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into <worktree>/.git/hooks   714: index.add([sm], write=True)                         # strict check only triggers here  git/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items)   732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path)                     # rejects ".git", too late  _to_relative_path only blocks `..`/absolute/out-of-tree paths; `.git` aliases are rejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) and runs at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll back what _clone_repo already wrote.  Version-dependent behavior: - 3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but the   hook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone). - 3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path does   not reject `.git`; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error at   all and the hook is planted silently.  ### Proof of concept   Setup:   evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload)   victim/  : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO              sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or `git init` with an empty              template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)  import git, os.path as osp try:     git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub")) except ValueError:     pass   # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened.            # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.  #### victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on every #### affected version. Any later checkout runs it: ####  git -C victim checkout <other-branch>   ->   the hook runs   ->   code execution  Verified live: - tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError from   git/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, and   `git checkout` executed it. - 3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was planted   and executed by `git checkout`.  ### Impact  Arbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from an attacker-influenced `path` ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in `.git/hooks`, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any service that derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests a submodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feeds `path` into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing that fails: it correctly rejects the `.git` path, but only after the submodule has already been cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes the unsafe path was blocked.  Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule `path`; (2) the target hook name is free in `.git/hooks`, true for minimal/CI/container checkouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the default sample hooks present, `git clone` refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.  Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.

> **A note on the referenced files.** This report was submitted through GitHub's private > vulnerability reporting API, which carries no attachments. Every transcript this report leans > on is reproduced **inline above**, verbatim. The file names it mentions (`poc.sh`, `poc.log`, > per-case transcripts, `evidence.md`, `negative-controls.md`, blob-sweep tables) are the local > evidence bundle those inline excerpts were extracted from, with a checksum manifest. I am happy > to send the bundle by any channel you prefer, or to open a private fork — just say which. The > PoC scripts are self-contained and reproduce the result from a clean environment.  ---  **Affected:** `<= 3.1.62` — all published releases; also `main` @ `4905b4af` **Verified at runtime:** GitPython `3.1.62` with git `2.55.0` **Date:** 2026-09-10 **Reporter:** MAXI8594  ---  ## Threat model  | | | |---|---| | **Attacker** | anyone who can get the application to clone a URL they control. No account, no credential, no privilege in the consuming application. | | **Pre-need** | a repository they host, with `HEAD` pointing at a branch whose name is the payload. A `git push` to a plain git server is enough — no filesystem access to a server is required (`raw/06`). | | **Gets** | the contents of any file the application's process can read, returned in band through the exception. `/etc/passwd` recovered 34 of 34 lines. | | **Real-world likelihood** | **High.** The vulnerable consumer is six lines of ordinary code with no unusual configuration: `Repo.clone_from(user_url)` then `repo.active_branch.checkout()`. `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default. Cloning user-supplied URLs is the library's central use case — CI systems, repository importers, scanners and bots. |  **On severity relative to the sibling advisories.** GitHub, as CNA, scored the three prior advisories in this class at 6.5 / `PR:L` (CVE-2026-76217, CVE-2026-78678, CVE-2026-78679). This report asks for 7.5 / `PR:N`, and the difference is one measured fact: in those three, the application had to pass an attacker-influenced value into the API. Here it passes nothing — the clone materialises the hostile branch on its own and `repo.active_branch` returns it (`raw/02`). If that reading is not accepted, the `PR:L` path via `Repo.create_head()` is also real and lands at 6.5, matching the siblings.  ## Summary  `Head.checkout()` guards its `**kwargs` against unsafe Git options but never inspects its own positional argument — the branch name — which reaches the `git checkout` argv with no `--` separator. A repository whose default branch is named `--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` makes a consumer that merely clones it and checks out the default branch return the entire contents of that file to the caller.  This is the exact combination of two advisories the project already fixed:  - **CVE-2026-76217** (`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc`) — *"Arbitrary file read via `--pathspec-from-file` in   `IndexFile.remove()` **and `Head.checkout()`**"*. Fixed in 3.1.58 by commit `f2550b65`, which added   the guard to this exact method — but only for `**kwargs`. - **CVE-2026-78679** (`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg`) — *"`TagReference.create` positional reference   bypasses kwargs-only `--file` guard, enabling arbitrary file read (incomplete fix of 3af0c251)"*. Fixed in 3.1.59 by commit `1b0d2d9b`, which applied the   positional check to `git/refs/tag.py`, `git/diff.py`, `git/index/base.py` and `git/repo/base.py` —   but not to `git/refs/head.py:286`.  `f2550b65` states in its own commit message that the audit found the positional variant and applied it to `HEAD.reset` — 185 lines above `Head.checkout`, in the same file, in the same commit:  > "The audit also found that **reset's positional commit could carry the option before its argument > separator**. […] **Check reset's positional commit as well as keyword options**"  `HEAD.reset` got the fix. `Head.checkout` did not, and `1b0d2d9b` did not come back for it.  ## Affected Asset  | | | |---|---| | Package | `GitPython` (PyPI) | | Affected versions | **`<= 3.1.62`** — all published releases | | Latest release tested | `3.1.62` | | Also present on | `main` @ `4905b4af` | | Vulnerable file | `git/refs/head.py` | | Guard | line 286 — `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)` | | Sink | line 293 — `self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` | | CWE | CWE-88 (Argument Injection), CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path), CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information) | | CVSS 3.1 | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` → **7.5 High** |  The version range was established by **blob hash against every tag**, not by dates: the sink line `self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` — with no `--` separator — is present in `git/refs/head.py` in every tag from `0.3.1-beta2` through `3.1.62`. The `3.1.62` blob is byte-identical to `main`: `7f563374ef9e018b3d5f95054498e8591e112ce2`. Full sweep in `raw/07-blob-version-sweep.txt`.  The kwargs-only guard first appears in **3.1.58**, so `3.1.58`–`3.1.62` is where "incomplete fix" applies; earlier releases have the same sink with no guard at all.  ## Vulnerability Details  ### Root cause  `git/cmd.py:1045` — `_option_candidates()` only inspects the positionals it is handed:  ```python @classmethod def _option_candidates(cls, args: Sequence[Any] = (), kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None) -> List[str]:     """Collect possible option spellings before command-line transformation."""     options = [         option for option in cls._unpack_args([arg for arg in args if arg is not None]) if option.startswith("-")     ] ```  So `_option_candidates([], kwargs)` means: *check the keyword arguments, never check the positional arguments this method puts on the command line.* That is fine when the method has no attacker-influenced positional, or when it separates them with `--`.  `git/refs/head.py:283-293` — `Head.checkout()` has neither:  ```python         if not allow_unsafe_options:             Git.check_unsafe_options(                 options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs),                 unsafe_options=Git.unsafe_git_pathspec_from_file_options,             )         kwargs["f"] = force         if kwargs["f"] is False:             kwargs.pop("f")          self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs) ```  `self` is the only positional. It serialises to the branch name, lands in the `git checkout` argv, and is not in the list the guard inspects. `_call_process` builds `args_list = opt_args + ext_args`, so keyword-derived options precede positionals — which is why the rest of the library puts `"--"` first (`Remote.fetch/pull/push`, `Repo._clone`, `Repo.archive`, `IndexFile.remove`, `Commit.count` all do). `Head.checkout` does not.  ### Why the branch name is attacker-controlled  Git accepts a refname whose branch component begins with `-` and contains `/` (`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`):  ``` >>> git check-ref-format 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'     exit=0  stderr=''     => un refname que empieza con '-' y lleva '/' es VALIDO para git  >>> git -C <bare> update-ref 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' beea87239099     exit=0  stderr='' >>> git -C <bare> symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'     exit=0     HEAD del bare = refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd     ref en disco como arbol jerarquico: True  >>> Repo.clone_from('file://<bare>', <victim>)   # la app solo clona     ramas LOCALES creadas por el clone, sin que nadie las pida:       refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd     repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'     coincide con el nombre hostil: True ```  The transcript above also shows the second half: `git clone` **materialises that branch locally on its own** when the remote `HEAD` points at it — the consuming application never asks for it.  A plain git server accepts the refname over `receive-pack`, with no `--force` and no special config (`raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`), so the attacker does not need filesystem access to a server — a `git push` is enough. That measurement, and the clone in `raw/02`, both use the `file://` transport, which exercises the same git wire protocol as `https://`; I did not test against a hosted forge, since that would mean writing to a third party.  ### Why the leak reaches the caller  The file contents are in `CommandError.__str__`, not only in the `.stderr` attribute (`git/exc.py`):  ```python         self.stderr = stderr_decode and "\n  stderr: '%s'" % stderr_decode or ""      def __str__(self) -> str:         return (self._msg + "\n  cmdline: %s%s%s") % (             self._cmd, self._cause, self._cmdline, self.stdout, self.stderr,         ) ```  So `logging.exception(...)`, `print(e)`, or simply **not catching** the exception all disclose the file. The developer does not have to know `.stderr` exists.  ### Full chain  ``` Repo.clone_from(<attacker URL>)   ↓  remote HEAD points at refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd   ↓  git clone creates that LOCAL branch unasked repo.active_branch                → Head with name = "--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd"   ↓ Head.checkout()                   git/refs/head.py:286 — guard inspects kwargs only   ↓  self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)   git/refs/head.py:293 — no "--" git checkout --pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd   ↓  git emits one `error:` per unmatched pathspec — one per line of the file GitCommandError → CommandError.__str__ → the consumer ```  ## Steps to Reproduce  Environment: GitPython 3.1.62, git 2.55.0, Linux x86_64, disposable venv. Everything local — temporary repositories and the `file://` transport. No remote hosts, no third-party repositories.  The bundled `poc.sh` runs all seven scenarios as a single unit and writes `poc.log` plus one file per scenario under `raw/`. Minimal manual reproduction:  ```bash python3 -m venv /tmp/gp && /tmp/gp/bin/python -m pip install gitpython==3.1.62  W=$(mktemp -d) git init -q -b main "$W/a"; echo x > "$W/a/f.txt" git -C "$W/a" add f.txt git -C "$W/a" -c user.email=a@b -c user.name=a commit -qm c git clone -q --bare "$W/a" "$W/a.git" SHA=$(git -C "$W/a.git" rev-parse HEAD)  # the attacker names their default branch after the file they want git -C "$W/a.git" update-ref   'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' "$SHA" git -C "$W/a.git" symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'  cat > "$W/consumer.py" <<'PYEOF' import logging, sys, git logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s") try:     repo = git.Repo.clone_from(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])   # user-supplied URL     repo.active_branch.checkout()                          # ensure a clean working tree except git.exc.GitCommandError:     logging.exception("clone failed") PYEOF  /tmp/gp/bin/python "$W/consumer.py" "file://$W/a.git" "$W/victim" ```  ### Raw Request  The real `git checkout` argv, captured by instrumenting `Git.execute` (`raw/01-real-argv.txt`). This is the command GitPython actually built — the branch name became an option:  ```   argv real : ['git', 'checkout', '--pathspec-from-file=/tmp/gpargv-9im8ao2d/SECRET.txt'] ```  ### Raw Response  Observed output (`raw/05-six-line-consumer.txt`, tail) — git emits one `error:` line per unmatched pathspec, which is one per line of the target file:  ``` error: pathspec 'mysql:x:958:958:MariaDB:/var/lib/mysql:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git error: pathspec 'flatpak:x:957:957:Flatpak system helper:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git error: pathspec 'wazuh:x:956:955:Wazuh Agent:/var/ossec:/usr/sbin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git error: pathspec 'jdownloader:x:955:954:jdownloader:/opt/JDownloader/:/bin/false' did not match any file(s) known to git error: pathspec 'cups-browsed:x:953:953:CUPS printer discovery:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git' ```  `raw/03-full-file-disclosure.txt` counts the recovery against the real file:  ``` Archivo objetivo: /etc/passwd  (34 lineas no vacias) [CASO] repo.active_branch.checkout()  — nadie paso un nombre de rama   repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'   -> GitCommandError. Lineas de /etc/passwd recuperadas: 34 de 34 ```  ## Impact  An attacker who can get an application to clone a repository they control reads any file the application's process can read, with the contents returned in band. `/etc/passwd` was recovered in full (34 of 34 lines) in the run recorded in `poc.log`.  The attacker needs **no account and no privilege in the consuming application**, and no configuration change anywhere: `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default, and the vulnerable consumer is six lines of ordinary code. This is the central use case of the library — CI systems, repository importers, scanners and bots that clone user-supplied URLs.  ### Impact precondition  **Holds if:** the consuming application clones a repository whose default branch name the attacker chose, and then calls `Head.checkout()` on it — most commonly as `repo.active_branch.checkout()`, which needs no branch-name input from the application at all.  **Source writer:** the attacker, via the remote repository's `HEAD` and refs. Verified two ways — `git update-ref` + `symbolic-ref` on a bare repository, and `git push` to a plain git server, which `receive-pack` accepts without `--force` or special configuration (`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`, `raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`). The application never writes the branch name; `git clone` materialises it.  **Observed in:** `validation/gitpython/head-checkout-positional-pathspec/` — GitPython 3.1.62 (latest release) with git 2.55.0, in the single run recorded in `poc.log` (2026-09-10T02:10:23-03:00). File read: `/etc/passwd`, 34 of 34 lines recovered by the caller.   ### Limits, stated plainly  - Only the full long spelling works, because a refname cannot contain a space and is therefore a   single argv token; `git` rejects the abbreviated forms. This was established while developing the   payload and is **not** part of the attached run — the run exercises the working spelling only. - The attacker must know an absolute path to the target file. - Lines are disclosed only when they do not match a path in the repository. With a one-file hostile   repository none of them do, so the attacker controls this condition too. - The full-file result was measured on **git 2.55.0**, where `git checkout` emits one `error:` per   unmatched pathspec. `GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` notes that `--pathspec-from-file` alone quotes only the   first line — that holds for `git rm`, which aborts with `fatal:` on the first. It does not hold for   `git checkout` on 2.55.0.  ## Negative control  Full statement of what each control isolates and what would invalidate it: `negative-controls.md`. Every batch opens **and closes** with a positive control; if the closing one does not fire, the batch is discarded.  **Positive control (opening and closing, 4 batches).** `Head.checkout(pathspec_from_file="/etc/passwd")` — the same payload via kwargs. Fires in every batch: `UnsafeOptionError: --pathspec-from-file is not allowed, use allow_unsafe_options=True to allow it`. This proves the guard exists, is active under the default, and recognises the option — so a null result elsewhere cannot be the instrument failing to reach the code.  **Negative control.** The identical call on a branch named `benigna`. One variable changes: the leading `-`. Result: `['git', 'checkout', 'benigna']`, no exception, 0 lines disclosed.  **Precision control — the asymmetry inside one file** (`raw/04-precision-control-reset-vs-checkout.txt`). The same payload against the two methods in `git/refs/head.py` that received the guard in the same commit, 185 lines apart:  ``` [CONTROL DE PRECISION] mismo archivo, mismo commit de fix, dos metodos   HEAD.reset(commit=PAYLOAD)  guard SI mira el posicional BLOQUEADO por el guard (--pathspec-from-file i fuga= 0 lineas  [OK]   Head.checkout()      guard NO mira el posicional     GitCommandError                                fuga=34 lineas  [OK] ```  `HEAD.reset` (`head.py:101`, `_option_candidates([commit], kwargs)`) blocks what `Head.checkout` (`head.py:286`, `_option_candidates([], kwargs)`) lets through. This rules out the alternative explanation that any string containing `--pathspec-from-file` reaching git would disclose the file.  ## Remediation  One line, consistent with what `f2550b65` already did for `HEAD.reset` in this same file:  ```python                 options=Git._option_candidates([self], kwargs), ```  **The other candidate was evaluated and rejected.** Writing `self.repo.git.checkout("--", self, **kwargs)` would match the `--` pattern used elsewhere in the library and would also cover future `git checkout` options — but it **changes the semantics and breaks the method**: in `git checkout -- <arg>`, everything after `--` is a *pathspec*, not a branch. The command would stop switching branches and start restoring files. The `--` pattern works for `fetch`/`pull`/`push`/`clone`/`archive`/`rm` because their positionals genuinely are non-branch operands; it does not transfer here.  For defence in depth, `Repo.create_head()` could reject branch names beginning with `-`, which would also close the weaker `PR:L` path. That is a separate, optional change.  ## Prior art and de-duplication  All GitPython advisories in the GitHub database were reviewed — `gh api advisories -f ecosystem=pip -f affects=GitPython -f per_page=100 --paginate` returns **47** (the same command without `per_page` returns only the first page of 30). `Head.checkout` appears in two rows, one of which (`GHSA-w672-…`) is a withdrawn duplicate, leaving one substantive advisory:  - **`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` / CVE-2026-76217** — same method, but the **kwargs** path   (`pathspec_from_file=…, pathspec_file_nul=True`), fixed in 3.1.58. That path is closed today; it is   the positive control in every batch of this report. The **positional** path is not covered by it.  Neighbours, none overlapping:  - **`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg` / CVE-2026-78679** — the same **class** (positional bypasses a kwargs-only   guard) in a different method, `TagReference.create`, fixed in 3.1.59 by `1b0d2d9b`. That is the   patch that did not come back to `head.py:286`. - **`GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v` / CVE-2026-67323** — precedent for "a value placed before the `--` with no   leading-dash check", in `Repo.iter_commits` / `Repo.blame`. Those sites now pass their positional   to the guard; this one does not. - **`GHSA-7545-fcxq-7j24` / CVE-2026-44243** — path traversal via ref names in the reference APIs.   Different sink (filesystem path construction) and different impact (write and delete), but it   establishes that attacker-influenced ref names is a premise this project has already accepted.  ### No open fix proposal  Searched across three surfaces, because `gh search issues` excludes pull requests: `gh search prs`, `gh search issues` and the raw `search/issues` API. **No open or closed issue or pull request proposes passing the positional to the guard in `Head.checkout`.** The three PRs that touch this guard (#2204, #2180, #2163) are all merged and none of them does it — #2204 is the PR that introduced *both* call sites in this file, one checking its positional and one not. Full matrix in `dup-check.md`.  ### The project's own tests carry the same asymmetry  `test/test_refs.py` exercises the guard for both methods, and covers exactly the difference this report is about:  - `HEAD.reset` — the **positional** is tested (lines 304-308). - `Head.checkout` — only the **kwargs** path is tested (lines 282-291).  So the positional variant is a case the suite already knows how to write; it just was not written for `checkout`. The docstring added by #2204 to `Head.checkout` states that `--pathspec-from-file` requires opt-in via `allow_unsafe_options` — which is precisely the guarantee the positional path does not deliver. Nothing in the project declares the positional acceptable here.  ### Why the one-line fix works, which is not obvious  `Reference.__str__` returns `self.name`, not `self.path`. `Reference.name` strips the first two path components (`reference.py:122-132`), so a `Head` constructed on `refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` passes `check_path` — the *path* does begin with `refs/heads/` — while `str()` yields the bare option. Passing `[self]` to `_option_candidates` makes the guard see that same serialised string, which is why the one-line change closes it.  ## Evidence  | File | What it establishes | |---|---| | `poc.sh` | driver — runs all seven scenarios as one unit | | `poc.log` | full transcript of the single reference run | | `raw/00-versions-and-source.txt` | version under test is the published one; guard and sink present; `def checkout(` appears once, so the sink line is unambiguous | | `raw/01-real-argv.txt` | real `git checkout` argv, captured by instrumenting `Git.execute` | | `raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt` | git accepts the refname; `Repo.clone_from` materialises it unasked | | `raw/03-full-file-disclosure.txt` | 34 of 34 lines of `/etc/passwd` recovered | | `raw/04-precision-control-reset-vs-checkout.txt` | `HEAD.reset` blocks what `Head.checkout` allows | | `raw/05-six-line-consumer.txt` | six-line consumer, verbatim; leaks when the exception is logged and when it is uncaught | | `raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt` | a plain git server accepts the refname over `push` | | `raw/07-blob-version-sweep.txt` | affected range by blob hash, tag by tag | | `negative-controls.md` | what each control isolates and what would invalidate it | | `evidence.sha256` | integrity of every raw file and script |  ## Disclosure  Reported privately through GitHub private vulnerability reporting. No third-party systems were touched: every repository in this report is a temporary local one, and all transport is `file://`.

## Summary  `Remote.pull()` in GitPython forwards its positional `refspec` argument directly to the `git pull` child process while its unsafe-option guard inspects only keyword arguments. An application that passes attacker-influenced data as the `refspec` (for example a user-supplied branch or refspec parameter in a web or CI service) can supply an option-shaped value such as `--upload-pack=<command>`. The value bypasses the `unsafe_git_pull_options` check, is placed after the `--` separator on the `git pull` command line, and is executed as the upload-pack program for local-path or SSH transports. This yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the calling process using the documented default arguments (`allow_unsafe_options=False`).  ## Root Cause  `Remote.pull()` is documented to reject dangerous options unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`, and `--upload-pack` is explicitly listed as such an option. The guard, however, only screens keyword arguments and never the positional `refspec`. The check builds its candidate list with `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, passing an empty list in place of the positionals, so the `refspec` value is never compared against `unsafe_git_pull_options = ["--upload-pack"]`. The normalized `refspec` is then forwarded verbatim to the `git pull` invocation. The leading `--` separator that neutralizes an option-shaped refspec for `git fetch` and `git push` does not protect `git pull`, because `git pull` re-forwards its trailing positionals to an internal `git fetch` without re-inserting a `--` separator, so the positional becomes an option to that internal fetch.  ```text Affected function: git.remote.Remote.pull Source: git/remote.py (guard at the check_unsafe_options call using _option_candidates([], kwargs); sink at the self.repo.git.pull("--", self, refspec, ...) invocation) ```  ## Impact  An attacker who controls the `refspec` value passed to `Remote.pull()` achieves arbitrary operating-system command execution as the process invoking GitPython, with no additional privileges and no user interaction, on the default code path. Exploitation requires that the pulled remote uses a transport that runs upload-pack on the local side, namely a local filesystem path or SSH; over HTTPS the `--upload-pack` value is inert because the server ignores a client-supplied upload-pack program. This transport requirement narrows the population of vulnerable deployments but does not add work for the attacker once a vulnerable target is reached. Working checkouts commonly use local-path or SSH origins, so the exposed population is substantial.  ## Proof of Concept  ```text Environment: GitPython from the affected source tree; system git 2.43.0. The pulled origin uses a local filesystem transport (protocol.file.allow=always for git >= 2.38). ```  Reproduction steps:  1. Create an origin repository reachable over a local-path transport. 2. In a consumer repository, register that origin and call `Remote.pull()` with an attacker-controlled refspec. 3. Observe that the injected command executes.  ```python import git repo = git.Repo("consumer")                 # has an origin using a local-path or ssh transport origin = repo.remote("origin") # Attacker-controlled refspec value; default arguments (allow_unsafe_options=False): origin.pull(refspec="--upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack") ```  ```text cmdline: git pull -v -- origin --upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack [attack]  marker created (RCE)      : True [isolate] upload_pack passed as KWARG blocked : True   (only the positional refspec escapes) [sibling] same value via git fetch  : safe            (pull-specific behavior) [control] benign refspec            : safe ```  ## Attack Chain  1. **Exposure:** An application calls `Remote.pull(refspec=<value>)` on the default path, where `<value>` is derived from attacker-influenced input such as a branch or refspec request parameter. 2. **Control:** The attacker supplies the string `--upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`. The value passes through `Git._unpack_args`, which only flattens and stringifies it, preserving the option shape. 3. **Path:** The protocol loop calls `Git.check_unsafe_protocols` on the value, which only matches remote-helper transport URLs (a `<transport>::` form) and does not flag an `--upload-pack=` token. 4. **Guard:** The unsafe-option guard calls `check_unsafe_options(options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs), ...)`. Because positionals are passed as an empty list, the positional `refspec` is never inspected against `unsafe_git_pull_options`. 5. **Primitive:** The value is forwarded to `git pull -v -- <remote> --upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`; `git pull` re-forwards the positional to an internal `git fetch` without a `--` separator, so it is honored as the upload-pack program. 6. **Result:** For a local-path or SSH transport, git executes `<command>` as the upload-pack program, giving arbitrary command execution as the calling process user.  ## Bypass Evidence  The relevant guard is `Remote.pull()`'s own `check_unsafe_options` call, present in the current released artifact. It is incomplete: it inspects `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, which only considers keyword arguments, so the positional `refspec` is never checked. This was confirmed empirically: passing the identical value as the `upload_pack=` keyword argument raises `UnsafeOptionError`, while passing it as the positional `refspec` does not, proving that only the positional escapes the guard.  The `--` separator on the `git pull` command line was tested as a possible mitigation and refuted: with system git 2.43.0, `git pull -- <remote> '--upload-pack=<cmd>'` executed the injected command, while the identical value supplied to `git fetch -- ...` and `git push -- ...` did not execute, because those subcommands honor the `--` terminator whereas `git pull` re-forwards positionals to an internal fetch without one. The `check_unsafe_protocols` transport check was also examined and does not flag the `--upload-pack=` token because it has no `<transport>::` form. No prior published advisory for this package addresses `Remote.pull`, the fetch or pull refspec positional, or `--upload-pack` injection via a refspec; the closest accepted issue covers the same class (a positional argument escaping a keyword-only guard) in a different function and sink.  ## Affected Versions  - `Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)` - `Package: GitPython` - `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.1.30` - `Latest release checked: 3.1.62 (PyPI); source verified against the 3.1.62 release tag` - `Fix status: not fixed in any released version or on the development branch`  The keyword-only pull guard together with the positional `refspec` sink is present in every released tag from 3.1.30 through the latest release 3.1.62, verified by inspecting the shipped `git/remote.py` in each tagged artifact. Version 3.1.30 introduced the `unsafe_git_pull_options` guard; the affected range is stated from that boundary under the incomplete-guard framing. Releases before 3.1.30 forward the `refspec` positionally with no unsafe-option guard and no `--` separator and are also exploitable, but the range is stated conservatively from the guard-introduction boundary. No fixed release exists.  ## Suggested Fix  Enforce the unsafe-option invariant on the positional `refspec`, not only on keyword arguments. The guard should build its candidate list from the actual forwarded positionals (for example by passing the normalized refspec list into `Git._option_candidates` alongside `kwargs`) so that an option-shaped `refspec` such as `--upload-pack=...` is rejected with `UnsafeOptionError` unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`. The same correction should be verified for any other reference or refspec forwarding path that relies on the keyword-only guard. As an interim mitigation without a code change, callers should validate or reject refspec values that begin with `-`, avoid passing untrusted data as the `refspec`, and prefer HTTPS remotes where a client-supplied upload-pack program is inert.  Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

### Summary  This is a residual of GHSA-g5vv-9gxw-82hx / CVE-2026-87819. The 3.1.60 fix made `Actor._from_string` regex-free, but `parse_actor_and_date` still runs `_re_actor_epoch` on the same author/committer/tagger line one step earlier. That pattern backtracks quadratically when the trailing epoch or timezone is missing or malformed, so the same class of slow parse is still reachable in 3.1.62.  ### Details  `git/objects/util.py:322`:  ```python _re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") ```  `.+?` and `(.*)` can both absorb the same run of spaces, and the required ` (\d+) ([+-]\d+)` tail is only checked after them. On a long line with no valid tail, the search retries every split point.  It is called from `parse_actor_and_date` (`git/objects/util.py:335`), which runs on the author and committer lines in `Commit._deserialize` (`git/objects/commit.py:917`, `:931`) and on the tagger line in `git/objects/tag.py:129`.  The published payload (letters plus an unterminated `<`) is fast on 3.1.62. Replacing the letters with spaces is not:  | author line (after `author `) | 2 KB | 8 KB | 32 KB | |---|---|---|---| | `'a'*n + ' <'` (advisory payload) | 0.0 ms | 0.1 ms | 0.4 ms | | `' '*n` | 28 ms | 453 ms | 7,700 ms | | valid line, long name (control) | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms |  Cost grows about 16x for each 4x increase in length.  ### PoC  ```python import time from git.objects.util import parse_actor_and_date  line = "author " + " " * 32000 t = time.perf_counter() parse_actor_and_date(line) print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")   # ~7 s on 3.1.62 ```  End to end, reading `Commit.author` on a commit object whose author line is 32 KB of spaces followed by any malformed tail (no epoch, no timezone, non-numeric epoch, or bad timezone) takes about 7.2 s per access. The same line with a valid `1191999972 -0700` tail takes 1.3 ms.  Note for reproducing: `git hash-object -t commit -w` refuses such an object (`missingEmail`), so the test object was written with `--literally`. A remote can still serve one, because `fetch.fsckObjects` and `transfer.fsckObjects` default to false. This is the same delivery model as CVE-2026-87819 ("craft a commit object with a malformed author field").  ### Impact  CPU exhaustion (CWE-1333) in any application that uses GitPython to read commits or tags from an untrusted repository: CI tooling, repository scanners, code-hosting integrations. Each access to `Commit.author`, `Commit.committer` or `TagObject.tagger` on a crafted object costs seconds, and a repository can contain many such objects.  ### Suggested fix  Match the leading field name with `.[^ ]*` instead of `.+?`. Both stop at the first space after the first character, but `.[^ ]*` cannot overlap the following `(.*)`, so the backtracking disappears:  ```python _re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") _re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$") ```  Verification on current main (73a72c9):  - Differential over 368 actor lines (real-world shapes plus edge cases): 0 differences in match groups for either regex. - `' '*n` at 64 KB: 32,170 ms before, 0.98 ms after. Valid lines are unchanged (0.01 ms). - The existing test suite gives the same pass/fail set with and without the change - The new regression test, `test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear`, fails on the old pattern (8.4 s) and passes with the fix (0.5 s).  The full patch (fix plus regression test) is attached below.  ```diff diff --git a/git/objects/util.py b/git/objects/util.py index a68d701f..d8c0594d 100644 --- a/git/objects/util.py +++ b/git/objects/util.py @@ -319,8 +319,11 @@ def parse_date(string_date: Union[str, datetime]) -> Tuple[int, int]:      # Precompiled regexes -_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") -_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*)$") +# The leading field name ("author", "committer", "tagger") is matched with ``.[^ ]*`` rather than +# ``.+?``: both stop at the first space after the first character, but ``.[^ ]*`` cannot overlap the +# following ``(.*)``, so a line with no valid trailing epoch/offset no longer backtracks quadratically. +_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") +_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$")      def parse_actor_and_date(line: str) -> Tuple[Actor, int, int]: diff --git a/test/test_util.py b/test/test_util.py index cf4299d5..e1631420 100644 --- a/test/test_util.py +++ b/test/test_util.py @@ -22,6 +22,7 @@ from git.cmd import dashify  from git.objects.util import (      altz_to_utctz_str,      from_timestamp, +    parse_actor_and_date,      parse_date,      tzoffset,      utctz_to_altz, @@ -571,6 +572,30 @@ class TestUtils(TestBase):              Actor("name last another", "some-very-long-email@example.com"),          )   +    def test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear(self): +        # A long author line whose trailing epoch/offset is missing or malformed used to make +        # _re_actor_epoch backtrack quadratically: ~7 s per Commit.author access for a 32 KB line. +        # The parse result must be unchanged; only the time spent reaching it should move. +        for tail in ("", " notanumber -0700", " 1191999972", " -0700", " 1191999972 xx"): +            line = "author " + " " * 32000 + tail +            start = time.perf_counter() +            actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date(line) +            self.assertLess(time.perf_counter() - start, 1.0) +            self.assertEqual(epoch, 0) +            self.assertEqual(offset, 0) + +        # Well-formed lines, including one with a long name, still parse exactly as before. +        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date( +            "author Tom Preston-Werner <tom@mojombo.com> 1191999972 -0700" +        ) +        self.assertEqual(actor, Actor("Tom Preston-Werner", "tom@mojombo.com")) +        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1191999972) +        self.assertEqual(offset, 25200) + +        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date("author " + "a " * 16000 + "<a@b> 1 -0700") +        self.assertEqual(actor.email, "a@b") +        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1) +      @ddt.data(          ("name", ""),          ("name", "prefix_"), ```  Found with AI assistance (Claude) and verified by hand. ### Summary  GitPython has spent 2022-2026 rolling out two reusable guards method-by-method: `Git.check_unsafe_protocols(url)` (raises `UnsafeProtocolError` for `<transport>::` remote-helper URLs - CVE-2022-24439) and `Git.check_unsafe_options(...)` (raises `UnsafeOptionError` for denylisted option spellings - CVE-2023-40267, CVE-2026-42215, CVE-2026-67323). Three wrapper methods that build a `git` argv from caller-controlled values still have **neither**:  1. **`Git.ls_remote`** (git/cmd.py:1128-1143) - checks options (:1139-1141) but forwards the URL positional unchecked; no `allow_unsafe_protocols` parameter exists. The same URL through `clone_from` raises `UnsafeProtocolError`. 2. **`Repo.merge_base`** (git/repo/base.py:895-936) - forwards `**kwargs`/`*rev` to `self.git.merge_base` with no guard; guarded sibling `iter_commits` sits 12 lines up. Its exception handler additionally swallows every non-128 `GitCommandError` into `[]`, masking the injection. 3. **`IndexFile.move`** (git/index/base.py:1092-1168) - forwards `**kwargs` to `git mv` twice (:1147, :1167); guarded sibling `remove()` is 23 lines above.  Verified unfixed on `main @ a54d159` (2026-09-21), post-dating latest release 3.1.62 (2026-09-07) - all three sites re-verified today.  ### Impact  **Site 1 (`ls_remote`)** - RCE conditional on the victim git transport policy. The common 'probe first, then clone' pattern (`Git(...).ls_remote(attacker_url)`) with an `ext::sh -c ...` URL executes arbitrary commands when the victim git permits the ext transport: dynamically verified with `protocol.ext.allow=always` (marker executed). git >= 2.38.1 stock config refuses the transport (`fatal: transport 'ext' not allowed`, rc 128) - GitPython adds no defense-in-depth and surfaces a bare `GitCommandError`. Environments on git < 2.38.1 are exposed with stock config - the exact population CVE-2022-24439 was scored against.  **Sites 2/3** - latent argument-injection surface: caller kwargs flow 1:1 into the `git` argv before operands and `--` (cmd.py:1850 `opt_args + ext_args`), and `execute_kwargs` (incl. `shell=True`/`env` - the CVE-2023-40267 Windows mechanism) passes through unguarded. Today `git merge-base`/`git mv` expose no exec option, so we claim the missing-guard class (vendor-settled by CVE-2026-67323, which bundled archive/ls_remote/iter_commits/blame in one advisory), not direct RCE.  ### Dynamic verification (today; GitPython main @ a54d159, git 2.55.0, Linux)  | # | Call | Result | |---|---|---| | T1 | `repo.git.ls_remote('ext::/tmp/gp_touch.sh')`, stock config | git refuses (rc 128); **no `UnsafeProtocolError` from GitPython** | | T1b | same + victim config `protocol.ext.allow=always` | **marker created - arbitrary command executed** | | T2 | `repo.git.ls_remote('.', upload_pack=...)` | blocked by cmd.py:1141 (options-side fixed - protocol-side is the residual gap) | | T3 | `repo.merge_base('main','side', upload_pack=...)` | **not blocked**; argv `git merge-base --upload-pack=... main side`; rc 129 silently converted to `[]` | | T4 | `repo.index.move(['f1','f2'], output=...)` | **not blocked**; option reaches `git mv` (rc 129) |  ### Coverage matrix (main @ a54d159)  `check_unsafe_protocols`: 7 call sites (`_clone`, `archive`, `set_url`, `create`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`) - none on `ls_remote`. `check_unsafe_options`: 24 call sites incl. `ls_remote`, `iter_commits`, `IndexFile.remove` - absent on `merge_base` and `move`.  ### Precedents (same repo, same guard family)  - **CVE-2022-24439 / GHSA-hcpj-qp55-gfph** (critical): `check_unsafe_protocols` on the clone path - Site 1 is the same `ext::` primitive on a sibling API. - **CVE-2023-40267 / GHSA-pr76-5cm5-w9cj** (critical, 'incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24439'): `check_unsafe_options` - unguarded kwargs to argv treated as RCE (`shell=True` on Windows). - **CVE-2026-42215 / GHSA-rpm5-65cw-6hj4** (high, fixed 3.1.47): underscored-spelling bypass - rollout still active in 2026. - **CVE-2026-67323 / GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v** (high, 8.4, fixed 3.1.51): added `check_unsafe_options` to `archive`/`ls_remote`/`iter_commits`/`blame`; its PoC is literally `repo.git.ls_remote('.', upload_pack=...)`. Establishes that a wrapper missing the check is itself a vulnerability. This report is the residual gap of that rollout: `ls_remote` got options but not protocols; `merge_base`/`move` got neither.  ### Recommended fix (existing helpers, 1-3 lines per site)  1. `Git.ls_remote`: `if not allow_unsafe_protocols: self.check_unsafe_protocols(args[0])` + new `allow_unsafe_protocols: bool = False` (the `_clone` pattern, base.py:1536-1538). 2. `Repo.merge_base`: `check_unsafe_options(Git._option_candidates(list(rev), kwargs), unsafe_options=self.unsafe_git_revision_options)` (the `iter_commits` pattern); stop masking non-128 statuses. 3. `IndexFile.move`: the `remove()` pattern with `unsafe_git_pathspec_from_file_options`.  One advisory, three affected methods, severity anchored on Site 1 - mirroring CVE-2026-67323's bundling.

### Summary `Repo._clone()`'s handling of `separate_git_dir` never disables `Git.polish_url()`'s environment-variable expansion, unlike every other caller of that helper that handles attacker-influenced data. Since `separate_git_dir` can be derived from an attacker-controlled `.gitmodules` submodule name, a completely ordinary `clone` + `submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True)` on a malicious repository expands an environment variable of the attacker's choosing and exposes its value both as a persistent on-disk directory name and, whenever DEBUG-level logging is enabled (a common CI/verbose-logging configuration), in a `Popen(...)` log line that is not redacted the way credential-bearing arguments are.  ### Root cause / Details `git/repo/base.py`'s `_clone()` has:  ```python sep_dir = kwargs.get("separate_git_dir") if sep_dir:     kwargs["separate_git_dir"] = Git.polish_url(sep_dir) ```  This is the only remaining `Git.polish_url()` call site handling attacker-influenced data that does not pass `expand_vars=False` (there is one other unguarded call site, `clone_path` at line 1537, but its input is the caller's own local destination path, not attacker-controlled). The sibling fixes for `GHSA-94p4-4cq8-9g67`/`GHSA-rwj8-pgh3-r573` added `expand_vars=False` to `clone_url` (5 lines below this one, in the same function), `git/repo/base.py:1599`, `remote.py:814`, and `submodule/base.py:686` — this one did not receive it. (`submodule/root.py` also currently sets `expand_vars=False` at a related call site, but that was added incidentally by a later, unrelated commit, not as part of these security fixes.) `Git.polish_url()`'s docstring itself says: "Disable this for values obtained from an untrusted source, such as remote URLs." Its non-Cygwin branch does plain `os.path.expandvars()` on the entire string, including embedded variables anywhere in an absolute path.  `separate_git_dir` reaches `_clone()` from `Submodule._clone_repo()` (`git/objects/submodule/base.py`) as `module_abspath = osp.join(parent_repo.git_dir, "modules", name)`, where `name` is the raw `.gitmodules` submodule section name — fully attacker-controlled content of a cloned repository. `_validated_name()` (added by the fix for `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc`) only rejects names that are absolute, contain a drive letter, or contain `..` path components; it does not reject `$`. `_need_gitfile_submodules()` is true for git ≥ 1.7.5, i.e. the default path for virtually every real-world installation.  ### Reproduction (live, against real, unmodified GitPython code, no monkeypatching) Built a hostile repository with a plain, ordinary git command: `git submodule add --name '$GPY_SECRET_MARKER' ../evil_submodule sub`. Set an environment variable in the "victim" process (standing in for a real CI secret such as `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`): `GPY_SECRET_MARKER=AKIA_TOTALLY_FAKE_BUT_SECRET_LOOKING_VALUE_12345`. Then ran the exact ordinary workflow the `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc` advisory's own PoC also uses:  ```python repo = Repo.clone_from(evil_parent_url, victim_clone_dir) repo.submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True) ```  Observed result (`ls .git/modules/`):  ``` .git/modules/AKIA_TOTALLY_FAKE_BUT_SECRET_LOOKING_VALUE_12345/   (a full git repo: HEAD, config, objects/, refs/, hooks/) ```  The literal `$GPY_SECRET_MARKER`-named directory was never created — only the expanded one exists, proving expansion happened before the value reached the `git clone --separate-git-dir=...` subprocess argument. The persistent, expanded-name directory under `.git/modules/` is itself the primary disclosure channel — it survives on disk for as long as the clone does. A second, independent channel: with the `git.cmd`/`git.repo.base` loggers at DEBUG level (a common CI/verbose-logging setting, not requiring any special flag), GitPython's own `Popen(...)` debug log line prints the fully expanded `--separate-git-dir=<value>` subprocess argument verbatim — `remove_password_if_present()` only redacts URL passwords/Authorization headers, not path-style arguments like this one, so the expanded value is not scrubbed. (The call also fails downstream with an `OSError`/`FileNotFoundError` referencing the original, unexpanded name, since `_write_git_file_and_module_config()` looks for a directory using the pre-expansion name — but that error message itself does not contain the expanded/secret value.)  **Control**: the same call with an ordinary (no `$`) submodule name succeeds normally and creates `.git/modules/<name>` as expected — isolating the gap to submodule names containing environment-variable syntax specifically.  ### Already-known check Checked all 35 published `gitpython-developers/GitPython` security advisories in full text. `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc` covers the same `name` → `.git/modules/<name>` path but for path-traversal (`../../..`), not variable expansion. `GHSA-59cr-6r3x-644w` covers the sibling `path` field reaching unguarded `os.makedirs()`. `GHSA-94p4-4cq8-9g67`/`GHSA-rwj8-pgh3-r573` cover `expand_vars`, but only on URL arguments. `git log -p -S "separate_git_dir" -- git/repo/base.py` shows neither fix commit touches this line; it is unchanged since its 2016 introduction (commit `57d05379`).  The closest topical match is `GHSA-8mcc-hrx5-hvxc` ("`clone_from()`/`clone()` omit `--separate-git-dir` from `unsafe_git_clone_options`") — already fixed, and its own text discusses this same `_clone()` handling of `separate_git_dir`. That fix only added `--separate-git-dir` to the `unsafe_git_clone_options` denylist, which gates the direct-kwarg vector; `Submodule._clone_repo()` explicitly sets `allow_unsafe_options=True` for the gitfile-submodules path, unconditionally bypassing that exact denylist (confirmed: the reproduction above succeeds against current `main`, which already has that fix). The bug this report describes is independent of that denylist — the *value* itself is expanded via `os.path.expandvars()` regardless of the denylist outcome — so the two are distinct, but flagging the relationship explicitly since a reviewer would otherwise reasonably ask about it.  No advisory describes environment-variable expansion via the internal `separate_git_dir` path.  ### Suggested fix Add `expand_vars=False` to the `Git.polish_url(sep_dir)` call in `_clone()`, matching the four other call sites already fixed for the same class of issue.  ### Verification level Reproduced in a real environment: plain Linux, unmodified GitPython from current `main`, real git ≥ 1.7.5 behavior, an ordinary `git submodule add` + `clone` + `submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True)` workflow with no non-default configuration or monkeypatching required. Causation isolated via a control group (identical workflow, ordinary submodule name, no expansion).  ### AI Use Disclosure AI (Claude) was used as a tool under my direction for code review, code summarization, and script development. A human reviewed and verified the AI-generated results before submission.  Credit: please use "baeseungwon1010" (github.com/baeseungwon1010).
